title: Civilian Protection in Islamic Law and the Biblical Tradition
subtitle: Why Islamic law forbids targeting innocent people, and how the Quran's war passages fit together
summary: The Prophet's prohibition on killing women and children gives Muslims a clear reason to reject attacks on protected people. Classical law also debated protected categories, night raids, and incidental harm; it was not simply identical to modern humanitarian law. Those difficulties must be faced while keeping the central moral claim: a sacred cause cannot turn the deliberate murder of protected people or betrayal of safety into worship.

seo.metaTitle: Civilian Protection in Islamic Law and the Biblical Tradition
seo.metaDescription: Islam forbids deliberately killing civilians. Quran 9:5 addresses hostile Arabian groups after notice in an ongoing conflict, not peaceful civilians.

sections.title: A Cause Is Not Righteous if It Erases the People It Harms
sections.body:
Islam places limits on Muslim force, not only on the force used by enemies. [Sahih al-Bukhari 3015](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3015) records the Prophet's prohibition after a woman was found killed during a campaign. Quran 9:6 requires safety and passage for someone seeking protection.

These protections matter precisely during conflict. They are not earned by agreeing with Islamic belief, and they cannot be removed by declaring an entire people guilty.

sections.title: Defense Without Transgression
sections.body:
The Quran states:

وَقَٰتِلُوا۟ فِى سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلَّذِينَ يُقَٰتِلُونَكُمْ وَلَا تَعْتَدُوٓا۟ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُعْتَدِينَ

'Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not like transgressors' (Quran 2:190). The command identifies an enemy engaged in fighting and immediately sets a moral limit. The Quran also recounts the rule given to the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul unjustly is as though he had killed all humanity (Quran 5:32). Elsewhere it requires kindness and justice toward peaceful non-Muslims and acceptance when an enemy genuinely inclines toward peace. Together, these teachings make war exceptional and restraint obligatory.

sections.title: Quran 9:5: Context Helps, but It Does Not End the Debate
sections.body:
Quran 9:5 addresses conflict with Arabian polytheists. The neighboring verses preserve faithful treaties (9:4) and require protection and safe passage (9:6). A contextual reading connects the command with hostile groups and rejects treating it as an order to kill every non-Muslim.

Broader classical interpretations also existed. [Ibn Kathir's commentary](https://quran.com/at-tawbah/5/tafsirs/en-tafisr-ibn-kathir) records expansive fighting and abrogation claims and ties release in the verse to embracing Islam. It would be misleading to say every classical interpreter limited the passage to modern-style self-defense or equal civic coexistence.

That is a serious debate about the scope of warfare. It does not authorize a private person to kill neighbors or make the Prophet's explicit protection of women and children disappear. [Jihad and Just-War Theory](/articles/jihad-and-just-war-theory) addresses the wider question.

sections.title: A Clear Prohibition With Historically Debated Boundaries
sections.body:
The prohibition in [Sahih al-Bukhari 3015](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3015) and [Sahih Muslim 1744b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1744b) concerns killing women and children. Classical jurists discussed participation in fighting and the status of other groups, including adult men, religious recluses, and workers.

Their categories were not identical in every detail to the modern legal category of civilian. We can affirm the explicit prohibition without inventing unanimity on every later classification. Contemporary application must also honor binding covenants, protections, and applicable law rather than import an isolated old rule into a different setting.

sections.title: The Hard Case: The Night-Raid Report
sections.body:
[Sahih Muslim 1745a](https://sunnah.com/muslim:1745a) addresses women and children harmed in night attacks and replies that they are of the enemy people. Classical jurists read it alongside the explicit prohibition to distinguish unintended casualties from deliberate targeting. The report should not be hidden behind a claim that the sources recognize no such difficult cases.

That distinction does not make every death called 'accidental' acceptable. A morally serious application must consider whether the objective and method are lawful, what harm is foreseeable, and what precautions or safer alternatives exist. This is not a promise that every premodern ruling matches every modern legal test; it is a refusal to let incidental-harm arguments erase protection altogether.

sections.title: The Comparison Must Use One Moral Standard
sections.body:
Matthew 5:44's command to love enemies is a genuine resource for Christian ethics. Biblical conquest passages raise different historical and theological questions; Christians do not all read them as standing commands for modern armies.

Islam's case should therefore rest on its own protections and their defensible application, not on selecting the hardest biblical passage while concealing its own. A Muslim's treatment of an enemy is accountable to God even when criticism of the enemy is justified.

sections.title: Protection Must Survive Anger and Victory
sections.body:
Islam gives Muslims strong grounds to condemn terror against protected people, honor guarantees of safety, and restrain their own side. Its sources and legal history also require honest study of hard cases. Calling the whole subject either limitless violence or an exact copy of modern humanitarian law misrepresents it.

For a seeker, the positive invitation is to place power under moral accountability rather than tribal loyalty. Read [Rights of Non-Muslims](/articles/rights-of-non-muslims) next for how that duty extends beyond the battlefield to ordinary coexistence.

quranVerses.arabic: وَقَٰتِلُوا۟ فِى سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلَّذِينَ يُقَٰتِلُونَكُمْ وَلَا تَعْتَدُوٓا۟ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُعْتَدِينَ
quranVerses.translation: Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you but do not transgress. Indeed. Allah does not like transgressors.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: مِنْ أَجْلِ ذَٰلِكَ كَتَبْنَا عَلَىٰ بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ أَنَّهُۥ مَن قَتَلَ نَفْسًۢا بِغَيْرِ نَفْسٍ أَوْ فَسَادٍۢ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ فَكَأَنَّمَا قَتَلَ ٱلنَّاسَ جَمِيعًۭا وَمَنْ أَحْيَاهَا فَكَأَنَّمَآ أَحْيَا ٱلنَّاسَ جَمِيعًۭا ۚ وَلَقَدْ جَآءَتْهُمْ رُسُلُنَا بِٱلْبَيِّنَٰتِ ثُمَّ إِنَّ كَثِيرًۭا مِّنْهُم بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ لَمُسْرِفُونَ
quranVerses.translation: Because of that, We decreed upon the Children of Israel that whoever kills a soul unless for a soul or for corruption [done] in the land - it is as if he had slain mankind entirely. And whoever saves one - it is as if he had saved mankind entirely. And our messengers had certainly come to them with clear proofs. Then indeed many of them, [even] after that, throughout the land, were transgressors.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: إِلَّا ٱلَّذِينَ عَٰهَدتُّم مِّنَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَنقُصُوكُمْ شَيْـًۭٔا وَلَمْ يُظَٰهِرُوا۟ عَلَيْكُمْ أَحَدًۭا فَأَتِمُّوٓا۟ إِلَيْهِمْ عَهْدَهُمْ إِلَىٰ مُدَّتِهِمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُتَّقِينَ
quranVerses.translation: Excepted are those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists and then they have not been deficient toward you in anything or supported anyone against you; so complete for them their treaty until their term [has ended]. Indeed, Allah loves the righteous [who fear Him].
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: فَإِذَا ٱنسَلَخَ ٱلْأَشْهُرُ ٱلْحُرُمُ فَٱقْتُلُوا۟ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ حَيْثُ وَجَدتُّمُوهُمْ وَخُذُوهُمْ وَٱحْصُرُوهُمْ وَٱقْعُدُوا۟ لَهُمْ كُلَّ مَرْصَدٍۢ ۚ فَإِن تَابُوا۟ وَأَقَامُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَءَاتَوُا۟ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ فَخَلُّوا۟ سَبِيلَهُمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَفُورٌۭ رَّحِيمٌۭ
quranVerses.translation: And when the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists wherever you find them and capture them and besiege them and sit in wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they should repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, let them [go] on their way. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: وَإِنْ أَحَدٌۭ مِّنَ ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ ٱسْتَجَارَكَ فَأَجِرْهُ حَتَّىٰ يَسْمَعَ كَلَٰمَ ٱللَّهِ ثُمَّ أَبْلِغْهُ مَأْمَنَهُۥ ۚ ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّهُمْ قَوْمٌۭ لَّا يَعْلَمُونَ
quranVerses.translation: And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the words of Allah. Then deliver him to his place of safety. That is because they are a people who do not know.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

bibleVerses.text: But of the cities of these peoples, that Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance, you shall save alive nothing that breathes; but you shall utterly destroy them: the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite; as Yahweh your God has commanded you; that they not teach you to follow all their abominations, which they have done to their gods; so would you sin against Yahweh your God.
Now go and strike Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and don’t spare them; but kill both man and woman, infant and nursing baby, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.’”

He went up from there to Bethel. As he was going up by the way, some youths came out of the city and mocked him, and said to him, “Go up, you baldy! Go up, you baldy!” He looked behind him and saw them, and cursed them in Yahweh’s name. Then two female bears came out of the woods, and mauled forty-two of those youths.
But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you,

Remember what Amalek did to you by the way as you came out of Egypt; how he met you by the way, and struck the rearmost of you, all who were feeble behind you, when you were faint and weary; and he didn’t fear God. Therefore it shall be, when Yahweh your God has given you rest from all your enemies all around, in the land which Yahweh your God gives you for an inheritance to possess it, that you shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under the sky. You shall not forget.
but the field, when it goes out in the Jubilee, shall be holy to Yahweh, as a devoted field. It shall be owned by the priests.

faq.question: Does Quran 9:5 command Muslims to kill all non-Muslims?
faq.answer: No. Treaty protection and asylum in 9:4 and 9:6 rule out that reading. Classical commentators nevertheless differed over how broadly 9:5 authorized state warfare. A responsible answer acknowledges that debate without giving private people any license to attack non-Muslims.

faq.question: Does Islam forbid killing civilians?
faq.answer: The Prophet explicitly forbade killing women and children, and Islamic law contains substantial protections for people outside fighting. Classical categories and exceptions were not identical to every modern civilian classification. None of this makes attacks on protected people lawful simply because of religion or nationality.

faq.question: What about accidental civilian deaths in war?
faq.answer: The night-raid report in Sahih Muslim 1745a was read by jurists as addressing unintended rather than deliberate killing. It is a difficult case, not a blank check. Calling harm accidental does not remove the need to assess lawful purpose, foreseeable danger, precautions, and safer alternatives.

faq.question: Can individuals declare jihad or attack people they consider enemies?
faq.answer: No. Private violence, vigilantism, treachery, and attacks on civilians are forbidden.

furtherReading.title: Battlefields of the Prophet Muhammad: A Contribution to Muslim Military History
furtherReading.author: Muhammad Hamidullah
furtherReading.note: Historical study computing troop numbers and casualties across the Prophet's military campaigns from classical Arabic sources.

furtherReading.title: Did God Really Command Genocide? Coming to Terms with the Justice of God
furtherReading.author: Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan
furtherReading.note: Book-length philosophical and theological defense of reading the herem texts as bounded ancient Near Eastern conquest rhetoric (Baker Books, 2014).

furtherReading.title: The Lost World of the Israelite Conquest: Covenant, Retribution, and the Fate of the Canaanites
furtherReading.author: John H. Walton and J. Harvey Walton
furtherReading.note: Argues that herem means removal from ordinary use rather than literal annihilation in every instance, using internal biblical evidence (IVP Academic, 2017).

furtherReading.title: Arguing the Just War in Islam
furtherReading.author: John Kelsay
furtherReading.note: Scholarly study of the shari'a-based jurisprudential tradition on war and its rules protecting non-combatants (Harvard University Press, 2007).
